description: We are an engineering-focused team building an actionable, data-driven software solution using live NASA Earth Observation & satellite APIs. Our focus is on strong backend architecture, geospatial data processing, and turning raw satellite telemetry into automated real-world services rather than static dashboards. Looking for collaborators in full-stack dev, data pipelines, and UI/UX.
summary:
TerraFlare is a fire-detection analysis platform that reconciles NASA’s two main satellite fire records, MODIS and VIIRS, for India (2021 to 2026). It ingests FIRMS hotspot data, places detections on a common H3 hexagonal grid, and serves the results through a FastAPI backend to a React dashboard.

The two sensors differ in resolution and sensitivity, so their raw counts cannot be added. TerraFlare therefore uses NOAA-20 VIIRS as the single reference series and shows MODIS separately. It also calibrates MODIS against VIIRS (Terra and Aqua ratios) with held-out validation. The validation reports honest error: temporal error is 8 to 16%, but spatial transfer error is about 48 to 49%.

Its main strength is scientific honesty. Coverage comes from the date ranges of the ingested files, never from the absence of hotspots, so missing periods (such as early 2026) show as gaps, not zeros. Standard-processing history and provisional near-real-time data stay separate and are labelled. On top of this, the app offers fire-season shift analysis, spatial fire memory, and data-quality views, all written in plain language.

This matters because decisions about fire trends depend on trustworthy, clearly caveated data. Hotspots are thermal anomalies, not unique fires.
details:
TerraFlare turns raw NASA FIRMS hotspot files into a harmonized, auditable record of fire activity over India, and shows it in a dashboard. The pipeline has five steps:

  1. Ingest. Standard-processing (SP) files for 2021 to 2025 and near-real-time (NRT) files for 2026 are loaded for VIIRS (NOAA-20) and MODIS (Terra, Aqua). Records are cleaned and validated. NRT rows are kept only inside H3 resolution-5 cells that already contain an SP detection (12,108 cells), so NRT and SP describe the same footprint.
  2. Grid. Detections are aggregated per H3 cell per local solar day.
  3. Coverage. A per-sensor, per-day coverage table is built from the date ranges of the ingested files. Days inside a file range with zero detections are flagged “suspect” and treated as missing.
  4. Harmonize and calibrate. The harmonized series equals the NOAA-20 VIIRS observation, a single reference platform with no conversion. MODIS-to-VIIRS ratios (Terra 22.9, Aqua 10.6) are fitted on SP data only, using held-out validation, but they are not applied to the series. Separate FRP ratios are diagnostic only.
  5. Serve and display. A FastAPI backend exposes the results, and a React/TypeScript dashboard presents them.

Dashboard views

  • A fire overview with yearly VIIRS and MODIS totals shown side by side.
  • A MODIS vs VIIRS comparison with correlation (raw and deseasonalized) and co-detection rate.
  • A daily calendar heatmap.
  • Fire-season shift analysis.
  • Spatial fire memory (persistent, emerging, declining, sporadic cells).
  • A data-quality and provenance page.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Users can trust what they see. A missing period (for example 2026-01-02 to 2026-08-01) appears as a visible gap, never as zero fire.
  • Uncertainty is stated honestly. Temporal holdout error is 8 to 16%, but spatial transfer error is about 48 to 49%, and the interface says so.
  • Results come with plain-language explanations, so non-specialists can read them. Every output carries provenance.
  • The intended impact is better-informed analysis of fire trends and season timing by researchers, planners and the public, with fewer misreadings caused by mixing sensors or confusing “no data” with “no fire”.

Tools and technology

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, SciPy (bootstrap and Theil-Sen statistics), DuckDB and Parquet storage, H3 spatial indexing, pytest.
  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL, hand-built SVG charts.
  • Data: NASA FIRMS MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS C2 (NOAA-20) fire detections.
  • No special hardware was needed; everything runs on a laptop.

What is creative

  • It treats missing data as a first-class result. Gaps are drawn, labelled and excluded from analysis rather than hidden.
  • It reports the weak parts of its own method: the unfitted bridge, the spatial error, and “insufficient evidence” where five seasons cannot support a trend claim.
  • Hard rules are built into the code: never add MODIS and VIIRS, never infer coverage from absent detections, and keep SP and NRT separate.

Factors we considered

  • Sensor differences. The sensors differ in resolution (1 km vs 375 m), overpass time and sensitivity, so raw counts are not comparable.
  • Reference platform. A single reference platform avoids double-counting.
  • Provisional data. NRT data is not science-quality, so it is labelled provisional.
  • Gaps and edge days. Partial edge days and suspect-zero days are handled explicitly.
  • Short record. Five full years limit the strength of any trend claim.
  • Footprint. Results describe only the SP footprint, not all of India.
  • Thermal anomalies. A hotspot is a thermal anomaly, not a unique fire.

Current limitations

  • The 2026 gap (January to early August) is unresolved. It is either SP not yet released or a truncated download.
  • Some dashboard pages and the full test suite still need final verification.
